food.text: Around 1000 CE, Leopard's Kopje people crossed the Limpopo River and settled at Bambandyanalo, while the Zhizo moved west to settle Toutswe in modern-day Botswana. Some scholars believe relations between the two peoples were hostile and marked by military conflict, though others say they were more complex, both socially and politically. At Bambandyanalo the newcomers took up agropastoralism, growing crops and herding large cattle herds.
Farmers at Bambandyanalo grew sorghum, pearl millet, finger millet, ground beans, and cowpeas, aided by a wet period that boosted agricultural yield.

The Leopard's Kopje people at Bambandyanalo also took part in the Indian Ocean trade. They exchanged goods with Swahili city-states along the East African coast, linking their farming settlement to a wider trading world.

At Bambandyanalo, the Leopard's Kopje deliberately grazed their cattle herds on land belonging to other communities. This practice fostered socio-political relations between groups and increased their influence.

art.text: The Lydenburg heads, found in Lydenburg, South Africa and dated to around AD 500, are considered the earliest known African Iron Age sculptures south of the equator. They consist of seven earthenware sculpted heads alongside other pottery from the site.
The region's Gokomere culture, an eastern Bantu subgroup, flourished from about 500 to 800 AD. It is considered an early phase of the later Great Zimbabwe culture.

Toutswemogala Hill, an Iron Age settlement in what is now Botswana, was occupied from around the 7th century AD as part of an economy built on cattle-keeping. The remaining features include house-floors, large heaps of vitrified cow-dung and burials of the dead. Its outstanding structure is a stone wall.

The Upemba Depression in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has been populated almost continuously since the 5th century AD. It holds the largest known cemetery in sub-Saharan Africa, including the Kisalian Graves among more than 40 identified archaeological sites.

Around 1000 CE at Bambandyanalo, also called K2, in the Limpopo valley, women worked copper while men worked iron as part of a growing agropastoral community. This site was the capital of the Leopard's Kopje people before Mapungubwe rose to prominence.

The seven Lydenburg head sculptures, along with other pottery from the site, are intricately decorated. Archaeologists believe they may have been used for ceremonial or initiation purposes, though this remains speculative.

By the 10th century, the people of the Upemba Depression combined fishing, farming and metal-working, with metal-workers relying on traders to supply copper and charcoal for smelting. They exported salt and iron items and imported glass beads and cowry shells from the distant Indian Ocean.

Little is known today about the people who created the Lydenburg heads, since evidence about them is sparse. Even so, the sculptures point to a remarkable artistic heritage at Lydenburg from this early era.

Toutswemogala Hill sits within a broader cultural area of eastern Botswana, sharing similar ceramic production styles and timeframes with other archaeological sites nearby. This points to a shared regional tradition of craft-making among Iron Age communities.

science.text: The Gokomere or Ziwa cultures farmed the valley that would later hold Great Zimbabwe between the 4th and 7th centuries AD. They mined and worked iron there but built no stone structures, unlike the city that later rose on the same site.

Chibuene was a trading settlement on the Mozambican coast that took part in the Indian Ocean trade network. Large numbers of imported glass beads arrived there between 700 and 1000 AD, making it a key entry point for trade goods reaching the African interior.

In south-central Africa, copper ingots were already being used as a medium of exchange by as early as 1000 CE. The trading site of Ingombe Ilede in present-day Zambia later received such ingots, shaped into crosses, through inland trade routes.

The archaeological site of Bosutswe sits on a hill at the edge of the Kalahari Desert in Botswana and dates back to around 700 AD. Its early economy relied on raising cattle, sheep, and goats, before metalworking later became prominent there.

Glass beads found at Chibuene match deposits at sites up to 1500 kilometres away, including the Shashe and Limpopo river regions and the Zimbabwe Plateau. This shows how far Indian Ocean trade goods travelled inland by around 1000 AD.

Around 1000 CE, Leopard's Kopje people crossed the Limpopo River to settle Bambandyanalo. There, women worked copper and men worked iron as part of an agropastoral economy that also engaged in the Indian Ocean trade.

From the 10th century, states and chiefdoms in the Limpopo-Shashe Basin, south of the site that would become Great Zimbabwe, competed over gold and other goods. These goods were traded through the Indian Ocean trade network.

Chibuene engaged extensively in the Indian Ocean trade network as early as the eighth century AD, evidenced by imported glass. This made it one of the earliest southern trading sites to do so, well before many ports further north joined the network.

Chibuene's importance as a gateway linking the coast to the interior declined dramatically at the end of the first millennium. This downturn coincided with similar declines at Unguja Ukuu on Zanzibar and Tumbe on Pemba Island, sites further north.

politics.text: Societies speaking proto-Shona languages first emerged in the middle Limpopo River valley in the 9th century. From there they moved on to the Zimbabwean highlands.

The Gokomere culture, an eastern Bantu subgroup, flourished in what is now Zimbabwe from 500 AD to about 800 AD. Archaeological evidence indicates that it was an early phase of the Great Zimbabwe culture.

In the early Medieval Period, the Bakongo people were subjects of the Kingdom of Vungu. After its fall, they lived along the Atlantic coast of Central Africa in several kingdoms: Kongo, Loango, and Kakongo.

The Zimbabwean plateau became the centre of the Shona states that followed, beginning around the 10th century. This later led to the Shona civilisations that dominated the region from the 13th century.

Around the early 10th century, trade developed between the Zimbabwean plateau and Arab merchants on the Indian Ocean coast. This trade helped develop the Kingdom of Mapungubwe, which arose in the 13th century and was the precursor to the Shona civilisations.

The Gokomere culture likely gave rise to the modern Mashona people, which includes sub-ethnic groups such as the local Karanga clan. It also gave rise to the Rozwi culture, which originated as several Shona states.

Gokomere peoples were probably related to nearby early Bantu groups such as the Mapungubwe civilisation of north-eastern South Africa. Mapungubwe is believed to have been an early Venda-speaking culture, and the Gokomere were also related to the nearby Sotho.

culture.text: Waves of Bantu migrations from 2000 BC to 500 AD moved into the Congo Basin from the northwest, adding to and displacing the indigenous Pygmy populations in the south. The newcomers brought agriculture and iron-working from West Africa. The new metal tools revolutionized agriculture and animal husbandry, which led to the displacement of hunter-gatherer groups in the east and southeast. The Bantu language family became the main set of tongues for the Congolese, and the 10th century marked the final expansion of the Bantu in West-Central Africa.
culture.source_title: Pre-colonial history of the Democratic Republic of the Congo

culture.text: Cattle were central to daily life at Leopard's Kopje. Vitrified blocks of dung mark the edges of medieval cattle byres, and these kraals stood at the center of villages rather than at the edge. Larger herds appeared around the 10th century, thought to result from a developing gold trade.

The earliest settlement at Leopard's Kopje dates to the 9th century AD and is called the Zhizo phase. Excavators found glass and shell beads, copper bangles and large amounts of Zhizo pottery. Possible traces of manure suggest people kept goats or sheep.

In the Mambo phase at Leopard's Kopje, dating to the 10th and 11th centuries, archaeologists uncovered several hut floors and plastered courtyards. These gave them a sense of the settlement's layout. Figurines and cattle teeth were also found, along with evidence of an infant burial.
Strong evidence of iron smelting was found at the Mambo phase level of Leopard's Kopje. Bits of iron slag at the earlier Zhizo phase level suggest smelting there as early as the 9th century.

Only two glass beads turned up in Robinson's 1961 excavation at Leopard's Kopje. Both were cylindrical and blue-green, typical of phase II of the Leopard's Kopje culture. Huffman's later excavations found far more glass and shell beads dating back to the 9th century.
